title: The Deferred Repair
primary_metric: expected total dollars spent on the coolant system per year of ownership, comparing always paying for the preventive flush (The Standing Order) against paying only for the repair if a failure actually occurs (The Reactive Route)

options.A: The Standing Order -- approve the coolant flush every time the shop flags it, for as long as the car is owned
options.B: The Reactive Route -- decline the flagged coolant flush and pay for the repair only if the engine failure actually happens

deliverables.text: A three-year conditional-probability table for The Reactive Route: the Year 1 probability of a coolant-related failure, the Year 2 probability given the engine did NOT fail in Year 1, and the Year 3 probability given it did not fail in either Year 1 or Year 2 -- each pulled from Appendix B's sourced failure-rate data, with the conditioning stated in words for every row.

A compound-probability calculation, shown step by step, of the chance the engine fails at least once across all three years of continuous skipping -- computed from the complement of 'no failure in any of the three years,' using the Year 1/2/3 probabilities from D1.

An expected-annual-cost comparison table: The Standing Order's certain, constant per-year cost from Appendix A, next to The Reactive Route's probability-weighted expected cost for each of the three years (that year's failure probability multiplied by Appendix B's full repair cost), with the arithmetic for every cell shown.

A written filtering decision: using Appendix C's failure and repair data for the transmission fluid service and the cabin air filter, state which of those two flagged services would be treated the same way as the coolant flush and which would not -- defended with each service's own three-year failure probability, not the shop's tone or price alone.

An original visual display (a bar chart, a probability tree, or equivalent) comparing The Standing Order's three-year total cost against The Reactive Route's three-year expected cost, built from the D3 figures.

appendices.title: Comparison: The Other Two Flagged Services

balance.argument_a: The Standing Order converts an uncertain, potentially ruinous multi-year risk into a small, certain, budgetable annual cost of $473/yr [S1] -- once Appendix B's Year 1 (9%), Year 2 (13%), and Year 3 (20%) conditional failure probabilities are compounded (D2), the probability of at least one coolant-related failure across all three years of skipping comes out to roughly 36.7%, a real and non-trivial chance of a $2,938 repair bill [S4] Elena would have to absorb during the exact three-year window she has committed to keeping the car running for income. Even though The Reactive Route's computed expected cost ($411.32/yr) is currently lower than $473/yr by only a 13.0% margin, A's case is that eliminating that 36.7% tail risk entirely is worth paying a premium that thin, especially given how close the case's own numbers are to the point where A becomes the cheaper option outright (see modeling_assumptions[MA1].sensitivity).
balance.argument_b: Under MA1's own values (9%/13%/20%, 3-year average 14%), The Reactive Route's correctly-computed expected annual cost ($411.32) is genuinely lower than The Standing Order's certain cost ($473) -- B wins by the real expected-value math, not just by the naive trap. The trap is a DIFFERENT, wrong route to a similar-looking conclusion: a learner who compares the certain flush price directly against the certain repair price (ignoring the probability weighting entirely) will also land on 'just pay for the repair if it happens,' but for the wrong reason and with no way to know how close that answer is to flipping. The real quantitative case for B rests on D3's actual expected-cost comparison, which shows a real but thin 13.0% margin -- close enough to the ~16.1% average-probability flip point (see modeling_assumptions[MA1].sensitivity) that a Hero arguing MA1's schedule should be somewhat higher than assumed can legitimately flip the recommendation to A.
balance.margin_basis: margin = |expected_annual_cost(A) - expected_annual_cost(B)| / max(expected_annual_cost(A), expected_annual_cost(B)), where expected_annual_cost(A) = Appendix A's flush price ($473 [S1], paid every year, certain) and expected_annual_cost(B) = the average across the three years of (that year's Appendix B failure probability [MA1] x Appendix B's repair cost [S4, $2,938]). A = $473/yr. B = (0.09x2938 + 0.13x2938 + 0.20x2938)/3 = (264.42 + 381.94 + 587.60)/3 = $411.32/yr. margin = |473 - 411.32| / 473 = 13.0%. This is within the SPEC SS2 target 10-15% band. NOTE: because the Year 1-3 probabilities (MA1) are a stated Modeling Assumption rather than a sourced figure (no publishable per-year schedule exists -- see needs_source[] and RESEARCH_LOG.md), this margin is a designed property of the assumption's chosen values, not an empirical finding. The repair cost [S4] and flush price [S1] are real sourced figures; only the probability schedule is authored.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Year 1 / Year 2 (conditional on no Y1 failure) / Year 3 (conditional on no Y1-Y2 failure) probability of a coolant-related failure after a skipped flush
modeling_assumptions.basis: No source publishes a per-year conditional failure-probability schedule for a skipped coolant flush (confirmed by multi-tier search: RepairPal, CarMD Vehicle Health Index, AAA newsroom releases, Car Care Council, mechanic-trade press). Values escalate year over year consistent with the general, well-documented finding that deferred-maintenance risk compounds the longer a service is skipped, and keep the resulting 3-year compound probability (~36.7%) in the range repeatedly described qualitatively (without a precise figure) as 'a real, non-trivial risk' by mechanic-trade sources.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Under the current MA1 values (9%/13%/20%, 3-year average 14%), The Reactive Route's expected cost ($411.32/yr) is LOWER than The Standing Order's certain cost ($473/yr) -- B is the cheaper option by the raw expected-value math, at a 13.0% margin. The comparison flips to A -- The Standing Order becomes cheaper -- only if the 3-year average probability RISES above ~16.1% (473/2,938), e.g. a Hero arguing any one year's value (most plausibly Year 1's 9%, since it is the least-escalated and easiest to challenge upward) should be higher than assumed. This is the load-bearing, dilemma-flipping assumption in the case; margin is intentionally within the SPEC target 10-15% band, and close enough to the ~16.1% flip point (14% vs. 16.1%, roughly 2 points) that a modest, defensible upward challenge to the schedule can flip the recommended option from B to A.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Three-year cumulative probability of a billable transmission failure if fluid service is skipped
modeling_assumptions.basis: No source publishes this figure. Set lower than the coolant system's compound probability because independent mechanic-trade sources (Engine Builder Magazine, Transmission Digest) place complete transmission failure from never-changed fluid at 80,000-120,000 miles of neglect, well beyond a typical 3-year/~36,000-mile skip window, whereas coolant-system stress from a skipped flush accumulates immediately.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Even at 15%, expected cost against the $6,426 replacement cost is ~$964 over three years (~$321/yr), above the flush's own $313 price -- a higher assumed probability would materially strengthen the case for treating this service like the coolant flush in Challenge 3 (D4).

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Probability a skipped cabin air filter replacement causes a billable mechanical (not comfort/air-quality) repair
modeling_assumptions.basis: Every source found (CARFAX, FilterBuy, Premium Guard, Interfil, and general mechanic-trade coverage) describes the consequences of a skipped cabin air filter exclusively in terms of reduced airflow, uneven cooling, odor, and blower-motor strain 'in extreme cases' -- none quantifies or documents an actual billable mechanical-repair rate.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Not dilemma-flipping; no repair cost exists to weigh it against. Its role is pedagogical: Challenge 3 (D4)'s correct filtering answer is that the cabin filter does not deserve the coolant flush's treatment, on the evidence itself rather than on shop tone or price.

derived.notes: Figures computed from sensitivity_model.py, not restated in case.md (facilitator-only), kept here so FACILITATOR.md's Guide Notes stay checkable against a value of record instead of drifting silently.

single_lever_flip_thresholds.note: the relative increase (%) needed in EACH year's probability ALONE, holding the other two fixed, to flip the recommendation from B to A -- computed by sensitivity_model.py binary search.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: Year 2's conditional failure probability for one specific, already-in-service vehicle is a forecast of a future outcome, not a measurable present fact -- no amount of research today can know in advance whether Elena's specific coolant system will fail in year 2 of continued skipping. Tier 2 P5 found this dial flips the verdict to The Standing Order at +50% flex (19.5% vs the stated 13%).

Same forecast-of-a-future-outcome reasoning as y2_prob, compounded further into the future (Year 3 conditional on no failure in Years 1-2). Tier 2 P5 found this dial flips the verdict to The Standing Order at +50% flex (30% vs the stated 20%), and is the single most flip-sensitive dial in the case, consistent with modeling_assumptions[MA1].sensitivity.

Moved the guard comment to the end (matching every other case) and rewrote MA1/MA2/MA3's Sensitivity columns to describe fragility without stating the result, per skills/case-write/SKILL.md's 2026-08-13 rule.
